title: Cooling the Central Courtyard
description: Combine evidence across multiple sources to reach conclusions and recommendations that no single source can fully support alone.
subject: rla
author: Studo
reviewNotes: Focused Arguments practice reviewed for one-best-answer logic, evidence fidelity, close distractors, and source-faithful explanations.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported when Sources 1 and 3 are considered together?

options.text: Direct sun is associated with hotter courtyard surfaces, and many students report avoiding the unshaded stone area during hot midday hours.
The hot stone surface is the only reason any student avoids the courtyard.
options.whyWrong: The sources show an association and preferences, not a single proven cause for every student.

options.text: Students prefer lighter paving to shade canopies.
options.whyWrong: More shade received 54 percent, while cooler surfaces received 21 percent.

options.text: The courtyard air is exactly 14 degrees cooler in the shaded walkway.
options.whyWrong: Source 1 measured surface temperature, not air temperature.

explanation.whyCorrect: Source 1 provides the surface-temperature pattern and Source 3 provides student-use and preference evidence; together they support a cautious connection.
explanation.quickTip: A synthesis combines what different sources can support without turning association into proof.

questions.prompt: Which option has the strongest combined support for addressing the most immediate problem before the next hot season?

options.text: Option B, because young trees are guaranteed to create full shade by next season.
options.whyWrong: The memo says substantial tree shade would take several years.

options.text: Option C, because the supplier's claim proves the new paving will cool the campus.
options.whyWrong: The product has not been tested on campus, and supplier evidence alone does not establish local effect.

options.text: Option A, because measured shade is associated with much cooler surfaces and students most often request more shade, while the canopies can provide shade without waiting years for tree growth.
No option, because the sources do not prove exactly how many students will use the courtyard afterward.
options.whyWrong: Uncertainty about exact future use does not prevent making a reasoned, testable decision from the available evidence.

explanation.whyCorrect: This recommendation connects the measured shade difference, the dominant student preference, and the implementation timeline.
explanation.quickTip: A strong synthesis recommendation should be supported by more than one source and should respect practical constraints.

questions.prompt: What important limitation applies to using the student survey as evidence for choosing a project?

options.text: It includes no students at all.
options.whyWrong: The survey includes 510 students.

options.text: It reports preferences but does not show whether any specific project will actually increase courtyard use.
It measures surface temperature rather than opinions.
options.whyWrong: Surface temperatures come from Source 1; Source 3 is the opinion survey.

options.text: It asks only about tree planting.
options.whyWrong: It gives several possible changes, including shade and cooler surfaces.

explanation.whyCorrect: Preferences can guide priorities, but they are not outcome data from an implemented project.
explanation.quickTip: When synthesizing, keep each source in its proper role: preference evidence is not the same as performance evidence.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly synthesizes the cost and timing information in Source 2 with the other sources?

options.text: Trees are the cheapest listed option and may provide long-term benefits, but their slow shade development makes them less suited to the immediate shade need identified by the heat and student data.
Canopies are the cheapest option and therefore clearly the best long-term investment.
options.whyWrong: Canopies are the most expensive listed option, not the cheapest.

options.text: Lighter paving is already proven on campus to reduce surface temperature more than shade.
options.whyWrong: The college has not tested it on campus.

options.text: Because trees require irrigation, they cannot provide any environmental benefit.
options.whyWrong: The memo explicitly says trees could provide long-term environmental benefits despite maintenance needs.

explanation.whyCorrect: This statement combines the financial/timing tradeoff with the immediate problem identified in the other sources without erasing the long-term benefit.
explanation.quickTip: Synthesis often requires balancing evidence of need with constraints such as cost and timing.

questions.prompt: Which additional evidence would most improve a phased decision?

options.text: A campus vote on which option has the nicest name.
options.whyWrong: Naming preference does not test heat reduction or courtyard use.

options.text: A supplier advertisement repeating that light paving stays cooler.
options.whyWrong: Repeating the same untested claim adds little independent evidence.

options.text: Measurements of surface temperature and student use before and after installing one pilot improvement, taken at comparable times and weather conditions.
A list of tree species used in a distant city without any information about local climate or growth.
options.whyWrong: A species list alone would not test the effect of the chosen campus improvement.

explanation.whyCorrect: A before-and-after pilot would directly measure both physical conditions and actual student behavior, addressing limitations in the current sources.
explanation.quickTip: The best next evidence targets what the current sources cannot yet tell you.

questions.prompt: Which claim is NOT supported by the combined sources?

options.text: Shade is associated with lower measured surface temperatures in the courtyard.
options.whyWrong: Source 1 reports a consistent shaded-versus-unshaded difference.

options.text: A majority of surveyed students selected more shade as the change most likely to increase their use.
options.whyWrong: Source 3 reports 54 percent choosing more shade.

options.text: Trees may offer benefits but would not provide substantial canopy shade immediately.
options.whyWrong: Source 2 states both points.

options.text: Permanent canopies will definitely increase courtyard use by 54 percent.

explanation.whyCorrect: The 54 percent figure is a preference response, not a predicted percentage increase in actual use, and no canopy has been tested yet.
explanation.quickTip: Do not combine numbers from one source with an outcome from another unless the sources justify that connection.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest reason for a phased plan based on all three sources?

options.text: The sources establish an immediate heat/use concern but leave uncertainty about the real effect and long-term value of each specific intervention.
The sources contain so little information that no action can be justified.
options.whyWrong: There is meaningful evidence of heat differences, student preferences, costs, and timing.

options.text: A phased plan guarantees that every option will eventually be built.
options.whyWrong: Phasing allows testing; it does not require all options.

options.text: The facilities memo says student preferences should be ignored.
options.whyWrong: The memo does not make that claim.

explanation.whyCorrect: The evidence supports addressing the problem while also supporting continued measurement before larger or longer-term commitments.
explanation.quickTip: A phased recommendation is strongest when the need is credible but the best final solution is still uncertain.

questions.prompt: Which summary best represents the combined evidence without overstating it?

options.text: The courtyard is unusable in summer, and only permanent canopies can solve the problem.
options.whyWrong: The sources do not say the courtyard is unusable or that only one solution can work.

options.text: The data prove trees are a poor investment because they require maintenance.
options.whyWrong: Source 2 identifies long-term benefits as well as maintenance needs.

options.text: Measured shade is associated with cooler surfaces and students report wanting more shade; canopies could address that need quickly, while trees and cooler paving present different cost, timing, and evidence tradeoffs that may justify further testing.
Student preferences should determine the project because surveys are more reliable than temperature measurements.
options.whyWrong: The sources answer different questions and should be combined rather than ranked this way.

explanation.whyCorrect: This summary combines the strongest findings, identifies a plausible immediate response, and preserves uncertainty around alternatives.
explanation.quickTip: A synthesis summary should include the shared direction of the evidence and the major limits or tradeoffs.

curriculum.learningObjective: Combine evidence across multiple sources to reach conclusions and recommendations that no single source can fully support alone.
